claim: HIV-1 gp120/gp41 trimer undergoes a series of conformational changes to catalyze gp41-induced fusion of viral and cellular membranes.
source: The HIV-1 gp120/gp41 trimer undergoes a series of conformational changes in order to catalyze gp41-induced fusion of viral and cellular membranes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general background claim about HIV-1 fusion mechanism.

claim: The crystal structure shows gp41 locked in a fusion intermediate state by an MPER-specific neutralizing antibody.
source: Here, we present the crystal structure of gp41 locked in a fusion intermediate state by an MPER-specific neutralizing antibody.
evidence: The crystal structure determination is described in the abstract and methods, with data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: The structure illustrates conformational plasticity of six membrane anchors arranged asymmetrically with fusion peptides and transmembrane regions pointing in different directions.
source: The structure illustrates the conformational plasticity of the six membrane anchors arranged asymmetrically with the fusion peptides and the transmembrane regions pointing into different directions.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Hinge regions located adjacent to the fusion peptide and transmembrane region facilitate conformational flexibility that allows high-affinity binding of broadly neutralizing anti-MPER antibodies.
source: Hinge regions located adjacent to the fusion peptide and the transmembrane region facilitate the conformational flexibility that allows high-affinity binding of broadly neutralizing anti-MPER antibodies.
evidence: This is supported by structural observations in Figure 1E-G and binding data in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulation reveals a possible transition pathway into the final post-fusion conformation with central fusion peptides forming a hydrophobic core with flanking transmembrane regions.
source: Molecular dynamics simulation of the MPER Ab-stabilized gp41 conformation reveals a possible transition pathway into the final post-fusion conformation with the central fusion peptides forming a hydrophobic core with flanking transmembrane regions.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data presented in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: MPER-specific broadly neutralizing antibodies can block final steps of refolding of the fusion peptide and transmembrane region required for completing membrane fusion.
source: This suggests that MPER-specific broadly neutralizing antibodies can block final steps of refolding of the fusion peptide and the transmembrane region, which is required for completing membrane fusion.
evidence: This is supported by fusion assay data in Figure 2 and neutralization data in Table 2.

claim: HIV-1 Env is a prototypic class I fusion protein that shares common pathways in membrane fusion with class II and III viral membrane fusion proteins.
source: The HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein (Env) is a prototypic class I fusion protein that shares common pathways in membrane fusion with class II and III viral membrane fusion proteins (Baquero et al., 2015; Harrison, 2008; Kielian and Rey, 2006; Weissenhorn et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HIV-1 Env is expressed as a gp160 precursor glycoprotein that is cleaved into gp41 and gp120 by host furin-like proteases.
source: HIV-1 Env is expressed as a gp160 precursor glycoprotein that is cleaved into the fusion protein subunit gp41 and the receptor-binding subunit gp120 by host furin-like proteases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV-1 Env processing.

claim: Gp41 anchors Env to the membrane and associates non-covalently with gp120, forming a stable trimer of heterodimers.
source: Gp41 anchors Env to the membrane and associates non-covalently with gp120, thereby forming a stable trimer of heterodimers, the metastable Env prefusion conformation (Chen, 2019; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Conformational changes transform energy-rich prefusion Env into the low-energy, highly stable gp41 post-fusion conformation, providing free energy to overcome kinetic barriers for membrane fusion.
source: Orchestration of a series of conformational changes transforms energy-rich prefusion Env into the low-energy, highly stable gp41 post-fusion conformation, which provides the free energy to overcome the kinetic barriers associated with bringing two opposing membranes into close enough contact to facilitate membrane fusion (Harrison, 2008; Weissenhorn et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mechanistic studies.

claim: HIV-1 gp41 is composed of fusion peptide, fusion peptide proximal region, heptad repeat region 1, a loop region followed by HR2, MPER, transmembrane region, and a cytoplasmic domain.
source: HIV-1 gp41 is composed of several functional segments that have been shown or suggested to extensively refold upon fusion activation: the N-terminal fusion peptide (FP), a fusion peptide proximal region (FPPR), the heptad repeat region 1 (HR1), a loop region followed by HR2, the membrane proximal external region (MPER), the transmembrane region (TMR), and a cytoplasmic domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gp41 domain organization.

claim: Structures of native Env trimers in complex with broadly neutralizing antibodies revealed the conformation of the gp41 ectodomain lacking MPER in the native prefusion conformation.
source: Structures of native Env trimers in complex with different broadly neutralizing antibodies revealed the conformation of the gp41 ectodomain lacking MPER in the native prefusion conformation (Julien et al., 2013; Kwon et al., 2015; Lyumkis et al., 2013; Pancera et al., 2014; Stewart-Jones et al., 2016; Ward and Wilson, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple structural studies.

claim: Env interaction with CD4 results in opening of the closed prefusion trimer, including displacement of gp120 V1-V2 regions and changes in gp41.
source: Env interaction with CD4 results in opening of the closed prefusion trimer (Liu et al., 2008; Ozorowski et al., 2017), which includes the displacement of gp120 variable regions 1 and 2 (V1-V2) at the apex of the trimer and some changes in gp41 including extended and more compact HR1C helices, helical FP conformations (Wang et al., 2018) and accessibility of the MPER epitope for 10E8 interaction (Lee et al., 2016; Rantalainen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural and functional studies.

claim: Co-receptor binding is required for formation of a stable ternary complex of Env-CD4 with the co-receptor.
source: This is required for the formation of a stable ternary complex of Env-CD4 with the co-receptor (Chang et al., 2005; Dobrowsky et al., 2008; Shaik et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Co-receptor binding positions prefusion gp41 closer to the host-cell membrane.
source: Co-receptor-binding positions prefusion gp41 closer to the host-cell membrane (Chen, 2019) and induces a cascade of conformational changes in gp41.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: FP is repositioned by approximately 70 Å to interact with the target cell membrane, generating a 110 Å extended fusion-intermediate conformation.
source: First, FP is repositioned by ~70 Å (Pancera et al., 2014) to interact with the target cell membrane, generating a 110 Å extended fusion-intermediate conformation (Frey et al., 2008; Lai et al., 2014) that bridges the viral and the host cell membrane (Weissenhorn et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Refolding of HR2 onto HR1 leads to formation of the six-helix bundle core structure.
source: Subsequent refolding of HR2 onto HR1 leads to the formation of the six-helix bundle core structure (Caffrey et al., 1998; Chan et al., 1997; Weissenhorn et al., 1997), which pulls the viral membrane into close apposition to the host-cell membrane to set the stage for membrane fusion (Weissenhorn et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Membrane fusion generates a lipid intermediate hemifusion state that is predicted to break and evolve to fusion pore opening.
source: Membrane fusion generates a lipid intermediate hemifusion state, that is predicted to break and evolve to fusion pore opening (Chernomordik and Kozlov, 2005), which is regulated by six-helical bundle formation (Markosyan et al., 2003; Melikyan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mechanistic studies.

claim: Residues within FPPR, FP, MPER, and TM have been implicated in fusion.
source: Furthermore, residues within FPPR, FP, MPER, and TM have been as well implicated in fusion (Bellamy-McIntyre et al., 2007; Long et al., 2011; Peisajovich et al., 2000; Salzwedel et al., 1999; Shang et al., 2008) indicating that final steps in fusion are controlled by the conformational transitions of the membrane anchors into the final post-fusion conformation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: The presence of membrane anchors increases thermostability of gp41.
source: We show that the presence of the membrane anchors increases thermostability.
evidence: This is supported by circular dichroism data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing Tm of ~93°C.

claim: Gp41FP-TM reveals a thermostability of approximately 93°C.
source: Gp41FP-TM reveals a thermostability of ~93°C as measured by circular dichroism (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) indicating that the presence of FP and TMR increases the thermostability by ~7°C compared to gp41 lacking FP and TM (Buzon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by circular dichroism measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The presence of FP and TMR increases thermostability by approximately 7°C compared to gp41 lacking FP and TM.
source: Gp41FP-TM reveals a thermostability of ~93°C as measured by circular dichroism (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) indicating that the presence of FP and TMR increases the thermostability by ~7°C compared to gp41 lacking FP and TM (Buzon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with previous data cited from Buzon et al., 2010.

claim: Gp41FP-TM and 2H10 form a 3:1 complex with a KD of 2.1 ± 0.9 µM as determined by ITC.
source: To determine the stoichiometry of binding, we performed isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), which indicated that gp41FP-TM and 2H10 form a 3:1 complex with a KD of 2.1 ± 0.9 µM (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The structure of gp41FP-TM in complex with 2H10 was solved to a resolution of 3.8 Å.
source: The structure of gp41FP-TM in complex with 2H10 was solved by molecular replacement to a resolution of 3.8 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The asymmetric unit contained trimeric gp41FP-TM bound to one 2H10 nanobody.
source: The asymmetric unit contained trimeric gp41FP-TM bound to one 2H10 nanobody as indicated by ITC (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and ITC measurements.

claim: The six-helix bundle structure is conserved from HR1 residue A541 to HR2 residue L661 in all three protomers.
source: The six-helix bundle structure composed of three N-terminal and three C-terminal chains is conserved from HR1 residue A541 to HR2 residue L661 in all three protomers, and identical to previous structures (Chan et al., 1997; Weissenhorn et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison with previous structures.

claim: TMR and FP do not follow three-fold symmetry and their chains point into different directions.
source: However, TMR and FP do not follow the three-fold symmetry and their chains point into different directions (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: 2H10 interacts with chain C-A and stabilizes a partially extended MPER conformation including a kink at L669.
source: 2H10 interacts with chain C-A (Figure 1B and D) and stabilizes a partially extended MPER conformation, including a kink at L669 that positions the rest of MPER and TM (N674 to V693) at a 45° angle with respect to the six-helix threefold symmetry axis.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1B and D.

claim: The 2H10 epitope spans from residues Q658 to N671 and covers a total buried surface of 712.2 Å2.
source: The protomer A chain C 2H10 epitope spans from residues Q658 to N671, which is involved in a series of polar contacts with 2H10 covering a total buried surface of 712.2 Å2.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the 2H10-gp41 interface.

claim: Chain N-B forms a long continuous helix comprising FP, FPPR and HR1 from residues L518 to D589.
source: Chain N-B of the second protomer forms a long continuous helix comprising FP, FPPR and HR1 from residues L518 to D589 with the first six residues of FP being disordered.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Chain C-B folds into a continuous helix from M629 to A700 comprising HR2, MPER and TM.
source: Likewise, chain C-B folds into a continuous helix from M629 to A700 comprising HR2, MPER and TM (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Cα superimposition of chain C-B with MPER containing gp41 structures yields root mean-square deviations of 0.55 Å and 0.29 Å.
source: Cα superimposition of chain C-B with MPER containing gp41 structures (Buzon et al., 2010; Shi et al., 2010) yields root mean-square deviations of 0.55 Å and 0.29 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), indicating that the straight helical conformation is the preferred conformation in threefold symmetrical gp41.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The structure reveals flexible regions within FPPR and MPER.
source: Thus, the structure reveals flexible regions within FPPR and MPER.
evidence: This is supported by structural observations of different conformations in the three protomers.

claim: FPPR flexibility is supported by strictly conserved G528 and G531.
source: FPPR flexibility is supported by strictly conserved G528 and G531, while MPER has no conserved glycine residues.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and structural observations.

claim: The same kink within L661 to F673 has been observed in the MPER peptide structure and in complex with bnAb 10E8.
source: However, the same kink within L661 to F673 has been observed in the MPER peptide structure (Sun et al., 2008), and in complex with bnAb 10E8 (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The N-terminal FP residues 512 to 517 are disordered within the detergent micelle.
source: The N-terminal FP residues 512 to 517 are disordered within the detergent micelle.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure showing no electron density for these residues.

claim: Flexibility of the N-terminal FP region in the absence of membrane is consistent with NMR peptide structures that propose a flexible coil structure followed by a helical region starting at L518.
source: Flexibility of this region in the absence of membrane is consistent with NMR peptide structures that propose a flexible coil structure of the N-terminal part of FP in solution followed by a helical region starting at L518 (Serrano et al., 2017) as observed here.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous NMR studies and comparison with the crystal structure.

claim: FPPR and MPER act as hinges during gp41 refolding leading to membrane fusion.
source: Based on the flexible linkage of FP and TMR, we propose that both FPPR and MPER act as hinges during gp41 refolding leading to membrane fusion.
evidence: This is based on structural observations of flexibility in these regions.

claim: MD simulation confirmed that the gp41FP-TM structure is stable in a membrane environment during a 1 µs simulation.
source: In order to test whether the structure is influenced by the presence of the detergent, we probed its stability by MD simulation in a bilayer having the lipid composition of the HIV-1 envelope. This confirmed that the structure is stable in a membrane environment during a 1 µs simulation as only the flexibly linked FP of chain N-C moves within the bilayer during the simulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The tip of the 2H10 CDR3 dips into the bilayer during MD simulation.
source: The tip of the 2H10 CDR3 dips into the bilayer (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B), hence confirming the membrane-anchoring role of W100 for neutralization (Lutje Hulsik et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B and citation to previous study.

claim: Wild type 2H10 did not show significant neutralization against a panel of 10 clade B pseudo-viruses except for weak neutralization of NL4-3 and SF163P3.
source: Wild type 2H10 did not show significant neutralization against a panel of 10 clade B pseudo-viruses as reported previously (Lutje Hulsik et al., 2013), with the exception of some weak neutralization of NL4-3 and SF163P3.
evidence: This is supported by neutralization data in Table 2.

claim: 2H10-F and 2H10-RKRF show improved potency and breadth neutralizing six and eight pseudo-viruses, respectively.
source: However, both 2H10-F and 2H10-RKRF show improved potency and breadth neutralizing six and eight pseudo-viruses, respectively, albeit with less potency than wild-type bi-2H10 and bnAb 2F5, the latter recognizing an overlapping epitope (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by neutralization data in Table 2.

claim: Enhancing the membrane interaction surface did not increase detection of non-specific membrane binding in vitro.
source: Notably, enhancing the membrane interaction surface did not increase the detection of non-specific membrane binding in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by flotation assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: Monovalent 2H10 is a modest anti-MPER Ab that neutralizes by engaging MPER and the membrane.
source: This result confirms monovalent 2H10 as a modest anti-MPER Ab that neutralizes by engaging MPER and the membrane.
evidence: This is based on neutralization data and structural analysis.

claim: The 2F5-bound peptide structure cannot be superimposed onto gp41FP-TM without major clashes with adjacent gp41 protomers.
source: Although the 2H10 epitope overlaps with the 2F5 MPER epitope (Ofek et al., 2004), the 2F5-bound peptide structure (Ofek et al., 2004), cannot be superimposed without major clashes with adjacent gp41 protomers.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling and comparison.

claim: Cα superposition of 10E8 and LN01 structures in complex with MPER peptides demonstrated possible binding to gp41FP-TM chain C-C.
source: In contrast, Cα superposition of the structures of 10E8 and LN01 in complex with MPER peptides demonstrated possible binding to gp41FP-TM chain C-C (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: HCDR3 of both 10E8 and LN01 could make additional hydrophobic contacts with adjacent FP in the modeled binding mode.
source: Furthermore, HCDR3 of both 10E8 and LN01 could make additional hydrophobic contacts with adjacent FP in this binding mode.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling analysis.

claim: Immunoprecipitation confirmed interaction of gp41FP-TM with 10E8 and LN01 in vitro.
source: To confirm 10E8 and LN01 interaction, we performed immunoprecipitation of gp41FP-TM with both bnAbs, which confirmed their interaction in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: BLI revealed KDs of 0.2 nM for 10E8 and 34 nM for LN01 binding to gp41FP-TM.
source: We next validated binding by bio-layer interferometry (BLI) using gp41FP-TM as analyte. This revealed KDs of 0,2 nM for 10E8 and 34 nM for LN01 (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by BLI data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: BnAbs 10E8 and LN01 interact with gp41FP-TM with high affinity.
source: We conclude that bnAbs 10E8 and LN01 interact with gp41FP-TM with high affinity which may also stabilize an asymmetric gp41 conformation similar to the one observed in complex with 2H10 as suggested by the structural modeling (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by BLI data and structural modeling.

claim: One-µs MD simulation of the symmetric gp41 model in solution rearranges the membrane anchors such that they adopt a compact structure with trimeric FP interacting with adjacent TMs.
source: One-µs MD simulation of this model (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) in solution, rearranges the membrane anchors such that they adopt a compact structure with trimeric FP interacting with adjacent TMs.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The TMs kink at conserved Gly positions 690 and 691 during MD simulation in solution.
source: Furthermore, the TMs kink at the conserved Gly positions 690 and 691, as observed previously (Pinto et al., 2019; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and citation to previous study.

claim: 1-µs MD simulation in a bilayer resembling HIV-1 lipid composition relaxed the TM to its straight conformation.
source: In order to recapitulate the stability of the model in the membrane, we performed an additional 1-µs MD simulation of the model (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) in a bilayer resembling the HIV-1 lipid composition, which relaxed the TM to its straight conformation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The final structural model reveals tight packing of trimeric FP flexibly linked to HR1 by FPPR G525 to G527.
source: The final structural model reveals tight packing of trimeric FP flexibly linked to HR1 by FPPR G525 to G527 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the MD simulation-derived model shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HR2-MPER and TMR form continuous helices with the TMRs packing against trimeric FP in the post-fusion model.
source: HR2-MPER and TMR form continuous helices with the TMRs packing against trimeric FP (Figure 4A and C), which spans one monolayer (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the MD simulation-derived model shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: Most of the tryptophan residues within MPER have structural roles in the post-fusion conformation.
source: We therefore propose that most of the tryptophan residues have structural roles in the post-fusion conformation, hence providing an explanation for their functional role in fusion (Salzwedel et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the post-fusion model and citation to previous functional studies.

claim: The MPER epitopes recognized by 10E8 and LN01 are exposed in the post-fusion model, but antibody docking produced major clashes.
source: The MPER epitopes recognized by 10E8 and LN01 are exposed in the post-fusion model, but antibody docking to this conformation produced major clashes, consistent with no expected binding to the final post fusion conformation.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling and docking analysis.

claim: Lipid mixing was strongly attenuated when vesicles primed for fusion with N-MPER were incubated with bi-2H10 before addition of target vesicles.
source: Accordingly, lipid mixing was strongly attenuated when the vesicles primed for fusion with N-MPER were incubated with bi-2H10 before addition of the target vesicles (Figure 2A,+N-MPER/+bi-2H10, dotted trace).
evidence: This is supported by lipid mixing assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: N-MPER-induced membrane perturbations that can induce fusion with target membranes were inhibited by incubation with bi-2H10.
source: Thus, the N-MPER-induced membrane perturbations, which can induce fusion with target membranes, were inhibited by incubation with bi-2H10.
evidence: This is supported by lipid mixing assay data.

claim: 2H10-RKRF, bi-2H10, Fabs 2F5 and 10E8 inhibited both initial rates and final extents of lipid mixing induced by N-MPER.
source: Comparison of the kinetics of the lipid-mixing blocking effect of 2H10-RKRF, bi-2H10 and Fabs 2F5 and 10E8 showed that the four antibodies inhibited both the initial rates and final extents of lipid mixing induced by N-MPER (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by lipid mixing assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No inhibition of lipid mixing by 2H10-RKRF, bi-2H10 and 2F5 Fab was observed using a control MPER peptide lacking the 2H10 and 2F5 epitopes, while 10E8 still blocked lipid mixing.
source: Using a control MPER peptide lacking the 2H10 and 2F5 epitopes for vesicle priming no inhibition of lipid mixing by 2H10-RKRF, bi-2H10 and 2F5 Fab was observed while 10E8 still blocked lipid mixing, (Figure 2C) corroborating that the inhibitory effects depend on epitope recognition.
evidence: This is supported by lipid mixing assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Fab 10E8 inhibits lipid mixing in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Notably, Fab 10E8 inhibits lipid mixing in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by lipid mixing assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Inhibition of lipid mixing by 10E8 depends on direct membrane interaction.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of lipid mixing depends on direct membrane interaction since increasing hydrophobicity within the 10E8 Fab-membrane interface increases the inhibitory effect and decreasing 10E8 hCDR3 hydrophobicity abrogates lipid mixing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C), which is in agreement with neutralization determinants of 10E8 (Chen et al., 2014; Rujas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by lipid mixing assay data with 10E8 mutants shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: 10E8 blocked C-MPER-induced fusion more efficiently than N-MPER-induced fusion.
source: The complete 10E8 epitope encompasses C-terminal MPER residues plus N-terminal TM residues, the latter not included in the sequence covered by the N-MPER peptide. Consistent with this recognition pattern, 10E8 blocked C-MPER-induced fusion more efficiently than N-MPER-induced fusion, but was effective against both peptides.
evidence: This is based on lipid mixing assay data comparing N-MPER and C-MPER peptides.

claim: Lower concentrations of bi-2H10 compared to 2H10-RKRF were required to attain full blocking of the lipid-mixing process.
source: Following this trend, fusion inhibition levels estimated as a function of the antibody concentration confirmed the apparent higher potency exhibited by the bi-2H10 (Figure 2D). Lower concentrations of bi-2H10 compared to 2H10-RKRF were required to attain full blocking of the lipid-mixing process when measured 20 s (initial rates) or 300 s (final extents) after target-vesicle injection (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The higher inhibitory potency of bi-2H10 indicates an avidity effect.
source: The higher inhibitory potency of bi-2H10 indicates an avidity effect, which was also evident when the concentration of the epitope-binding fragments was plotted (Figure 2D and E, empty squares and dotted line).
evidence: This is based on comparison of dose-response curves for bi-2H10 and 2H10-RKRF.

claim: Bi-2H10 appeared to block the lipid mixing process efficiently even at 2H10:N-MPER ratios below 1:3 (mol:mol).
source: Moreover, bi-2H10 appeared to block the process efficiently even at 2H10:N-MPER ratios below 1:3 (mol:mol), consistent with the involvement of peptide oligomers in the promotion of membrane fusion.
evidence: This is based on dose-response analysis shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Both 2H10-RKRF and bi-2H10 neutralize HIV-1 at the stage of lipid mixing.
source: Based on these data, we suggest that both 2H10-RKRF and bi-2H10 neutralize HIV-1 at the stage of lipid mixing.
evidence: This is based on lipid mixing assay data.

claim: Gp41 containing its membrane anchors can adopt the predicted conformation with FP and TM inserted asymmetrically in cellular and viral membranes.
source: The fusion model predicts that six-helix bundle formation apposes viral and cellular membranes with FP and TM inserted asymmetrically in the cellular membrane and the viral membrane, respectively (Weissenhorn et al., 1999). Here, we show that gp41 containing its membrane anchors can adopt this predicted conformation, which is facilitated by flexible hinges present in FPPR and MPER corroborating their essential roles in membrane fusion (Blumenthal et al., 2012; Chen, 2019; Harrison, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and citations to previous models.

claim: The asymmetric conformation of membrane anchors suggests that bundle formation occurs before pore formation.
source: The asymmetric conformation of the membrane anchors suggest further that bundle formation occurs before pore formation as suggested previously (Markosyan et al., 2003; Melikyan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on structural observations and citations to previous studies.

claim: Final steps in fusion involve rearrangement and interaction of TM and FP.
source: The membrane-fusion model proposes further that final steps in fusion involves rearrangement and interaction of TM and FP (Weissenhorn et al., 1999), which is confirmed by the MD-simulation model of the post-fusion conformation.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and citation to previous model.

claim: The length of the rod-like post-fusion structure of 13 nm lacking the C-C loop is consistent with the gp41 structure lacking FP and TM.
source: Furthermore, the length of the rod-like post-fusion structure of 13 nm lacking the C-C loop is consistent with the gp41 structure lacking FP and TM (Weissenhorn et al., 1996).
evidence: This is based on structural measurements and citation to previous structure.

claim: FP is helical in the gp41FP-TM-2H10 complex and the MD-based post-fusion conformation.
source: FP is helical in the gp41FP-TM-2H10 complex and the MD-based post-fusion conformation, in agreement with NMR-based helical FP peptide models (Li and Tamm, 2007; Serrano et al., 2014), although β-strand structures of FP have been implicated in fusion as well (Apellániz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and citations to previous NMR studies.

claim: In native Env conformations, FP adopts multiple dynamic conformations that are recognized by broadly neutralizing antibodies.
source: In comparison, in native Env conformations, FP adopts multiple dynamic conformations that are recognized by broadly neutralizing antibodies (Blattner et al., 2014; Kong et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: In the post-fusion conformation, FP spans one monolayer of the membrane.
source: In the post-fusion conformation, FP spans one monolayer of the membrane, in contrast to suggested amphipathic helix-like interaction of FP with the outer layer of the target cell membrane, which may constitute a first contact with the cellular membrane (Han et al., 2001; Lai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on the MD simulation-derived post-fusion model.

claim: The coiled-coil interactions within FP and with TM in the post-fusion model explain the increased thermostability of gp41FP-TM compared to gp41 lacking FP and TM.
source: Furthermore, the coiled-coil interactions within FP and with TM in the post-fusion model explain the increased thermostability of gp41FP-TM compared to gp41 lacking FP and TM (Buzon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the post-fusion model and comparison with thermostability data.

claim: Refolding of FP and TM can liberate additional free energy to catalyze final steps of fusion.
source: We propose that refolding of FP and TM can liberate additional free energy to catalyze final steps of fusion.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and thermostability data.

claim: Replacement of TM by a phosphatidylinositol anchor inhibits membrane fusion.
source: Hence, replacement of TM by a phosphatidylinositol (PI) anchor inhibits membrane fusion (Salzwedel et al., 1993; Weiss and White, 1993), akin to the GPI-anchored HA inhibition of influenza virus membrane fusion at the stage of hemifusion (Kemble et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Combinatorial mutagenesis of conserved tryptophan residues within MPER was shown to affect syncytium formation, although individual mutations had no effect.
source: Combinatorial mutagenesis of the conserved tryptophan residues within MPER was shown to affect syncytium formation, although individual mutations had no effect (Muñoz-Barroso et al., 1999; Salzwedel et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mutagenesis studies.

claim: A W666A mutation was shown to affect infection.
source: However, in another study a W666A mutation was shown to affect infection (Bellamy-McIntyre et al., 2007), which was further enhanced in combination with a I675A mutation albeit without effect on syncytium formation (Narasimhulu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mutagenesis studies.

claim: W666, W670, and W678 likely play a structural role in stabilizing the post-fusion conformation.
source: Although it is not known at which stage of the fusion process the concerted action of the tryptophan residues is required, our structural model suggests that W666, W670, and W678 likely play a structural role in stabilizing the post-fusion conformation.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the post-fusion model shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Combinatorial mutations to leucine of the TM region comprising residues 683–693 affect virus infectivity.
source: Furthermore, combinatorial mutations to leucine of the TM region comprising residues 683–693 affect virus infectivity (Shang et al., 2008) in agreement with the proposed interaction of this part of the TM with FP in the post fusion model.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous mutagenesis study and structural analysis.

claim: Mutation of the conserved arginine at position 693 reduces fusion efficiency.
source: In addition, mutation of the conserved arginine at position 693 reduces fusion efficiency (Long et al., 2011), which however, may be related to its role in stabilizing a tilted TM conformation in the bilayer during the fusion process (Chiliveri et al., 2018; Pinto et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous functional and structural studies.

claim: The structural model of the post-fusion conformation is in agreement with proposed interactions of FPPR and MPER, as well as FP and TM.
source: Our structural model of the post-fusion conformation is further in agreement with proposed interactions of FPPR and MPER, as well as FP and TM (Louis et al., 2016; Reuven et al., 2012), thereby corroborating their essential roles at late stages of membrane fusion.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and citations to previous studies.

claim: Gp41FP-TM interaction with 2H10 stabilizes the asymmetric conformation of the membrane anchors.
source: Gp41FP-TM interaction with the 2H10 MPER-specific nanobody stabilizes the asymmetric conformation of the membrane anchors.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: Engineered increased 2H10 membrane binding improved breadth and potency of 2H10 neutralization.
source: In order to confirm that 2H10 is, indeed, a neutralizing MPER-specific nanobody, we engineered increased 2H10 membrane binding, which improved breadth and potency of 2H10 neutralization, in agreement with enlarged potency by increasing membrane-binding of 10E8 (Chen et al., 2014; Kwon et al., 2018; Rujas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by neutralization data in Table 2 and citations to previous studies.

claim: 2H10 is a modest anti-MPER neutralizing antibody whose neutralization potency is enhanced by using bi-2H10 with increased avidity and by increasing potential membrane interaction of the 2H10 monohead.
source: This confirmed 2H10 as a modest anti-MPER neutralizing antibody, whose neutralization potency is not only enhanced by using bi-2H10 with increased avidity (Lutje Hulsik et al., 2013), but also by increasing potential membrane interaction of the 2H10 monohead.
evidence: This is supported by neutralization data in Table 2 and citation to previous study.

claim: 2H10 inhibits membrane fusion at the stage of lipid mixing like 2F5 and other anti-MPER bnAbs.
source: Consistent with its neutralization capacity, 2H10 inhibits membrane fusion at the stage of lipid mixing like 2F5 and other anti-MPER bnAbs (Apellániz et al., 2014b; Huarte et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by lipid mixing assay data in Figure 2 and citations to previous studies.

claim: Gp41FP-TM interacts with MPER bnAbs 10E8 and LN01 in agreement with docking both structures onto the kinked protomer C chain C MPER epitope.
source: Moreover, gp41FP-TM interacts with MPER bnAbs 10E8 (Huang et al., 2012) and LN01 (Pinto et al., 2019) in agreement with docking both structures onto the kinked protomer C chain C MPER epitope.
evidence: This is supported by binding data in Figure 3 and structural modeling.

claim: The kink in the MPER peptide in complex with 10E8 is similar to the protomer C chain C kink and present in MPER peptide NMR structures.
source: Notably, the kink in the MPER peptide in complex with 10E8 (Huang et al., 2012) is similar to the protomer C chain C kink and present in MPER peptide NMR structures (Serrano et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and citations to previous studies.

claim: Ala mutations in the kink (671-674) affect cell-cell fusion and lower virus infectivity.
source: Furthermore, Ala mutations in the kink (671-674) affect cell-cell fusion and lower virus infectivity (Sun et al., 2014) corroborating the physiological relevance of the kinked conformation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous mutagenesis study.

claim: 10E8 and LN01 binding to gp41FP-TM stabilizes similar asymmetry as observed in the gp41FP-TM-2H10 structure by sampling the dynamic states of the membrane anchors.
source: We therefore propose that 10E8 and LN01 binding to gp41FP-TM stabilizes similar asymmetry, as observed in the gp41FP-TM-2H10 structure by sampling the dynamic states of the membrane anchors.
evidence: This is based on binding data and structural modeling.

claim: MPER antibodies can act all along the gp41 refolding pathway from blocking initial conformations of close to native Env up to a late fusion intermediate state.
source: Our data indicate that MPER antibodies can act all along the gp41 refolding pathway from blocking initial conformations of close to native Env (Carravilla et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2016; Rantalainen et al., 2020) up to a late fusion intermediate state that has already pulled viral and cellular membranes into close apposition.
evidence: This is based on structural and functional data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The long temporal window of action for MPER bnAbs is consistent with findings that the half-life of neutralization of MPER bnAbs is up to 30 min post virus exposure to target cells.
source: This opens a long temporal window of action for MPER bnAbs consistent with the findings that the half-life of neutralization of MPER bnAbs is up to 30 min post virus exposure to target cells (Shen et al., 2010; Williams et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous kinetic studies.

claim: Only one Ab per trimer may suffice to block final refolding of the membrane anchors required for fusion.
source: Furthermore, only one Ab per trimer may suffice to block final refolding of the membrane anchors required for fusion.
evidence: This is based on the stoichiometry observed in the crystal structure and ITC data.

claim: The presence of dynamic linkers connecting the core of viral fusion proteins with their membrane anchors FP and TM may be a general feature of all viral membrane fusion proteins.
source: Finally, the presence of dynamic linkers connecting the core of viral fusion proteins with their membrane anchors FP and TM may be a general feature of all viral membrane fusion proteins including the proposed flexible linkage of influenza virus HA FP to the central HA2 coiled coil (Benton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on structural observations and citation to a recent study on influenza HA.
